excerpt: Jules needs access to your repositories in order to work.
Use the "jules" label in an issue to assign a task directly in GitHub.
Jules runs in a virtual machine where it clones your code, installs dependencies, and modifies files.
Once you submit a task, Jules will generate a plan. You can review and approve it before any code changes are made.
Jules now automatically looks for a file named AGENTS.md in the root of your repository.
You’ll be notified when the task completes or needs your input.
Jules provides a diff of the changes. Quickly browse and approve code edits.
Jules creates a PR of the changes. Approve the PR, merge it to your branch, and publish it on GitHub.
You can use the API to create custom workflows, automate tasks like bug fixing and code reviews, and embed Jules's intelligence directly into the tools you use every day
In the Jules web app, go to the Settings page to create a new API key. You can have at most 3 API keys at a time.
The `automationMode` field is optional. By default, no PR will be automatically created.
To send a message to the agent:
Power users & agent-heavy workflows ... 300 ... 60

Jules runs in cloud-based VMs instead of on my local machine, making it much less useful than Claude Code. My projects have bespoke build scripts specific to my machine and environment.
I used Jules three times today, very impressive! It also handles coding-adjacent work. Good github integrations.
Jules was unable to complete the task in time. Please review the work done so far and provide feedback for Jules to continue.
Is Jules free of charge? Yes, for now, Jules is free of charge. Jules is in beta and available without payment while we learn from usage.
the agent is good, the UI horrible. 'Usability declines in inverse proportion to the number of vice-presidents who sign the release notes.'
its way better than the github thing in my experience it produces usable PRs
Used it didn't like it. Claude Code is far better because the active collaboration part.
The daily task limit went down from 60 to 15 (on the free plan) with this release. Personally I wasn't close to exhausting the limit because I had to spend time going back and forth, fixing its code.
I've been playing with it, and I've been generally not impressed. There are obvious annoying UI bugs and the output isn't very good for anything but the simplest problems.

Tried both Jules and Gemini CLI, heavily advertised and disappointing. Running it on any slightly more complex codebase, it will crash every few iterations and complain I have drained all the credits.
I've used this tool for a few months now and have been pretty impressed by it. It handles large quantities of tasks very well and is good at making tests for very specific/isolated functions.
I've been actually kind-of enjoying using Jules as a way of 'coding' my side project using my phone. By the time I get home in the evening I've got a few PRs to review.
I've tried using Jules for a side project, and the code quality it emits is much worse than GH Copilot, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code. It also had a tendency to get confused in a monorepo.
Jules quickly after a few messages/prompts just gets stuck in an endless loop like Gemini-cli does. The worst part is that there is no 'STOP' button to quickly get it out of the loop.
I gave Jules a try on a new, very unorganized Python project. It failed the first time, I gave it the error message and it fixed it. I was shocked it ran after that. Not bad for the free plan.

I've moved infrastructure to Railway and taught the customer to use Jules. They make their own PRs now, Railway spins up an environment with the changes. It works like 75% of the time. Huge time saver.
It's a shame Google picked the wrong system design for Jules. Claude Code's system design is clearly superior at this point.
Do people really find Jules useful? I find it needs babysitting much more than Cursor.
Was able to build a personal MCP server that connects to the Jules API, letting me dispatch tasks to Jules, from Copilot Chat in VS Code.
